prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: [val][adversarial] Long group header over tiny sub-columns (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 5 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Merged cells: "Model" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Benchmark accuracy on he" spans 3 col × 1 row; "Notes" spans 1 col × 2 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Model" · longest unbreakable word 45px · one-line width 45px
  col 2: header "Benchmark accuracy on held-out multilingual evaluation suite › EN" · longest unbreakable word 21px · one-line width 21px
  col 3: header "Benchmark accuracy on held-out multilingual evaluation suite › ZH" · longest unbreakable word 22px · one-line width 22px
  col 4: header "Benchmark accuracy on held-out multilingual evaluation suite › AR" · longest unbreakable word 21px · one-line width 21px
  col 5: header "Notes" · longest unbreakable word 63px · one-line width 581px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"poor","why":"The three numeric columns and Model take up much of the width, leaving Notes so narrow that sentences break into many short lines and make the data rows unnecessarily tall."},"B":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Notes reads comfortably, but the benchmark group is cramped: its heading wraps into five lines above three very narrow numeric columns."},"C":{"grade":"excellent","why":"The benchmark heading fits in two lines, the three scores have balanced widths, and Notes has enough room for a readable two-line sentence and a single-line final note."},"D":{"grade":"good","why":"The heading and scores are clear, but the wider numeric columns leave less room for Notes, making the final note wrap onto a second line."},"E":{"grade":"excellent","why":"The heading fits in two lines, the three score columns are evenly spaced, and Notes is wide enough to keep the final note on one line."},"F":{"grade":"good","why":"Notes and the scores read clearly, though the benchmark heading takes three lines and leaves a taller header than in C or E."}},"best":["C","E"],"confidence":"high","unsure":"C and E are very close; their small differences in column proportions do not produce a clear reading advantage."}
